newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Lamers sees EMU deal with France soon.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Lamers sees EMU deal with France soon.

text.p: The foreign policy spokesman in parliament for Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats predicted on Saturday that Germany and France would settle their differences over Europe's single currency before the Amsterdam summit began on Monday.

But Karl Lamers said Germany opposed costly job-creation programmes such as France has proposed because they ultimately failed to reduce unemployment. He said Bonn was convinced the way to fight joblessness was through structural reforms.

"We are convinced that programmes that raise expenditure are not sensible," Lamers told German Radio. "We have tried that in the past and it didn't work...Where is the added money going to come from without going further into debt?"
Lamers said in the past spending programmes only ended up raising inflation and interest rates, which was ultimately counterproductive to efforts to reduce unemployment.

"I am certain that we will find common ground," Lamers said. "It has been proven through countries that have successfully fought unemployment like the Netherlands that the only way to lower unemployment is with structural reforms."
Lamers said French and German officials were working intensively through the weekend to try to bridge the differences.

Kohl met French President Jacques Chirac and Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin in Poitiers, France, on Friday in an unsuccessful bid to reach agreement on the proposed jobs pact for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Jospin said the new French government was committed to a single currency but wanted a fundamentally new approach to monetary union.
France's demands for a focus on growth and jobs must be given the same importance as the stability pact limiting budget deficits after the launch of a single currency, he said.

France's new government, swept to power in an upset parliamentary election victory two weeks ago, raised its objections to the stability pact designed by Germany at an international meeting for the first time on Monday.

"I know that the French are under pressure for several reasons," Lamers said. "Especially because of the promises the new French government made during the campaign, promises that can be best explained by saying they didn't expect to win."
Lamers said Germany was now "doing everything we can" to meet the French demands but "not in a way that will we are convinced will not only accomplish nothing but cause even more problems".
Lamers said it was merely a question of time before the French government realised their jobs plans would not work.
"I am convinced they won't need any more time before the start of the Amsterdam summit on Monday," he said.
